edges.description: Extension of acute necrotizing infection into facial soft tissues produces stage 2 facial edema prior to frank gangrene.
Polymicrobial invasion directly causes rapidly spreading gangrenous necrosis of intraoral and facial soft and osseous tissues.
Putrefactive anaerobic bacterial metabolism and sloughing necrotic oral tissue generate extreme oral fetor (halitosis).
Acute necrotizing mucosal, soft-tissue, and periosteal destruction causes severe intraoral and facial pain.
Acute necrotizing polymicrobial infection elicits systemic febrile inflammation.
Necrotizing destruction of alveolar bone and periodontal support leads to exposure and loss of teeth.
Full-thickness sloughing of gangrenous oral and facial tissues heals by scarring, leaving severe facial disfigurement in survivors.
Acute masticatory inflammation and subsequent cicatricial contracture or bony ankylosis restrict jaw opening.
Destruction of lips, cheeks, jaws, and oral structures together with trismus impairs oral food intake, mastication, and swallowing.
Loss of lip, cheek, palatal, and dental structures with jaw restriction impairs articulation in survivors.
Impaired host defenses from malnutrition and infection permit antecedent oral lesions to progress to the polymicrobial gangrenous tissue necrosis that defines noma.
Untreated antecedent necrotizing gingival or mucosal ulceration breaches the intraoral barrier, allowing invasion by the anaerobic bacterial consortium to trigger rapid gangrenous tissue necrosis.
Malnutrition synergizes with endemic infections to induce host immunodeficiency.
Impoverished living conditions expose young children to inadequate nutrition and poor sanitation that compromise host immunity.
Endemic viral, parasitic, and retroviral infections act synergistically with malnutrition to deepen host cellular and mucosal immunodeficiency.
